title: Strongly-connected percolation on directed lattices
authors: M. E. J. Newman, P. Grassberger, R. M. Ziff
abstract: We study percolation on lattices with directed bonds, focusing on the behavior of strongly-connected percolation clusters -- clusters in which every site is reachable from every other along a directed path. We consider the two-dimensional square lattice and various globally isotropic arrangements of the directions of the bonds. Performing simulations using a range of algorithmic approaches, we calculate high-precision values for critical exponents, fractal dimensions, crossing probabilities, and percolation thresholds for bond percolation with each bond arrangement. We find that the critical behavior is in a distinctly different universality class from that of traditional undirected percolation, but that all bond arrangements appear to fall in the same universality class.
summary: This paper analyzes strongly-connected percolation on directed lattices, determining that its critical behavior belongs to a unique universality class different from standard undirected percolation. Using advanced simulation techniques and graph algorithms, the authors compare various bond arrangements and establish formal equivalences between different lattice models. The work is significant for understanding connectivity thresholds in anisotropic or directional physical systems.
main_problem: The study investigates percolation on lattices with directed bonds, specifically focusing on the properties of strongly-connected clusters.
main_result: Strongly-connected percolation exhibits critical behavior in a universality class distinct from traditional undirected percolation, although all tested bond arrangements fall into the same universality class.
method: The authors employed extensive numerical simulations and developed advanced graph algorithms (like Tarjan's) to calculate high-precision values for critical exponents and thresholds.
model_or_system: The model is bond percolation on two-dimensional square lattices with directed bonds, including specific arrangements like the Manhattan lattice, L-lattice, random diode, and square ice models.
key_observables: Percolation thresholds ($p_c$), critical exponents, fractal dimensions, crossing probabilities, and the hull dimension ($d_h$).
important_parameters: Bond occupation probability ($p$) and lattice size ($L$).
main_assumptions: The study focuses on cases where bonds point in a single direction, excluding bidirectional (resistor-diode) configurations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate strongly-connected clusters for various models; one figure maps bond percolation on the L-lattice to site percolation on a Manhattan lattice at 45 degrees.
paper_structure: The paper analyzes the definition of strong connectivity, details algorithmic approaches (Tarjan's algorithm) for cluster detection, presents results comparing critical exponents across different directed lattices, and discusses formal mappings between models.
why_interesting: While focused on classical percolation, the rigorous mathematical analysis of connectivity thresholds and universality classes provides foundational tools applicable to understanding phase transitions in complex quantum systems or network reliability studies.
